## Practice Problems

<details>
<summary>Design Task 1, Problem 1 (plug-in): a clamp cylinder bore</summary>

A weld-fixture clamp cylinder needs 900 N of clamping force at 6 bar line pressure, with the clamp motion happening on the extend stroke (full bore area governs, not the annulus). Find the minimum bore area and diameter, and check whether a standard 50 mm bore clears the 25% oversize floor.

**Solution:**

$$A_{min} = \frac{900}{6\times10^5} = 0.0015\ \text{m}^2 = 1500\ \text{mm}^2 \qquad d_{min} = \sqrt{\frac{4(1500)}{\pi}} = 43.7\ \text{mm}$$

A 50 mm bore gives $A_{bore} = \pi/4(50)^2 = 1963.5\ \text{mm}^2$, an oversize margin of $(1963.5/1500 - 1) = 30.9\%$ — inside the 25-50% guideline band, so 50 mm is a good selection.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 1, Problem 2 (design decision): standard size doesn't fit the band</summary>

A different application's minimum annulus area works out such that the next standard bore up gives only an 18% margin, and the one after that gives 95%. Which do you select, and what design change (other than accepting one of those two bores) might resolve the mismatch entirely?

**Answer:** Select the larger bore (95% margin) for the same reason worked through in this chapter's own example — an inadequate margin is a functional risk, while extra margin is a cost and packaging issue. Beyond simply accepting one of the two standard sizes, two other design changes are worth considering before committing to the oversized cylinder: increasing line pressure (if the plant's compressor and distribution system can support it) reduces the required bore area for the same force, potentially bringing the smaller standard size back into an acceptable margin; alternatively, if the mismatch is being driven by a marginal force requirement, revisiting whether that requirement itself has its own conservative padding (a common occurrence when several designers each add their own safety margin at different stages) may reveal the true requirement is lower than assumed.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 2, Problem 1 (plug-in): actual force with a lower efficiency factor</summary>

Using the same 50 mm/20 mm cylinder (theoretical retract force 989.6 N), estimate actual retract force with a more conservative combined efficiency factor of 0.70 (long tubing run, aging compressor system). Does it still clear the 550 N requirement?

**Solution:**

$$F_{actual} = 989.6 \times 0.70 = 692.7\ \text{N}$$

Yes — still comfortably above 550 N (26% margin), though noticeably tighter than the 45.7% margin found with the 0.81 efficiency factor used in the chapter's worked example.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 2, Problem 2 (design decision): a small-bore application with thin margin</summary>

A different, smaller cylinder (16 mm bore) shows only a 12% actual-force margin after applying a 0.70 efficiency factor — appropriate for its small bore per this chapter's guidance. The project is under cost pressure to avoid moving up a size. What are your options besides accepting the thin margin or upsizing the cylinder?

**Answer:** A few options worth exploring before either accepting the risk or paying for a larger cylinder: (1) shorten and straighten the tubing run and eliminate unnecessary fittings between the valve and cylinder to improve the pressure-drop half of the efficiency factor; (2) verify the valve itself isn't the bottleneck — an undersized valve (Design Task 4) contributes directly to the pressure-drop loss; (3) check whether the seal/friction specification can be improved (a cylinder with a lower-friction seal package, sometimes a manufacturer option, directly improves the friction half of the efficiency factor); (4) confirm the regulator is actually holding setpoint under the branch's real flow demand, not sagging due to being undersized itself (Design Task 5). Only after those are checked and the margin is still thin should upsizing the cylinder be treated as the remaining option — small-bore applications are exactly where this chapter flagged margin as most fragile, so a 12% margin here deserves more scrutiny than the same number would on a large-bore cylinder.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 3, Problem 1 (plug-in): air consumption at a faster rate</summary>

Using the same 50 mm/20 mm cylinder and 100 mm stroke, find the free-air consumption in SCFM if the cycle rate increases to 45 cycles/min.

**Solution:**

Free-air volume per cycle stays the same as the chapter's worked example, 2.5012 L (this doesn't depend on cycle rate). At 45 cycles/min:

$$Q_{NL/min} = 2.5012 \times 45 = 112.6\ \text{NL/min} \qquad Q_{SCFM} = \frac{112.6}{28.317} = 3.97\ \text{SCFM}$$

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 3, Problem 2 (design decision): compressor capacity check</summary>

The plant's existing compressor has 15 SCFM of uncommitted spare capacity. Engineering wants to add six more pick-and-place stations identical to this chapter's example (1.70 SCFM average each, from the chapter's worked example), each cycling continuously. Does the spare capacity cover it, and what should the engineer check beyond the raw SCFM sum?

**Answer:** Six stations at 1.70 SCFM average each sum to 10.2 SCFM, which is under the 15 SCFM spare capacity on paper — but average consumption alone isn't the whole picture. The engineer should also check: (1) whether these six stations' cycles are likely to overlap in time (if they're on a synchronized line, their peak/burst demand — the Cv-driving flow from Design Task 4, not the average — could spike well above the average sum, briefly starving other equipment on the same header even though the time-averaged number fits); (2) whether the "spare capacity" figure already accounts for existing leaks and inefficiencies in the current system (Design Task 6) — spare capacity calculated against a leaky baseline overstates what's actually available; (3) whether adding this load pushes the compressor's duty cycle high enough to affect its service life or trigger more frequent lead/lag staging in a multi-compressor plant. A comfortable-looking average-SCFM margin is a starting point, not a final answer.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 4, Problem 1 (plug-in): required Cv for a faster fill time</summary>

Using the same 50 mm bore extend-stroke fill (free-air volume 1.3593 L = 0.04800 ft³) and the same pressure conditions as the worked example, find the required Cv if the fill time requirement tightens to 0.08 s.

**Solution:**

$$Q_{burst} = \frac{0.04800}{0.08/60} = 36.0\ \text{SCFM}$$

$$C_v = \frac{36.0}{22.48}\sqrt{\frac{1.0 \times 530}{15 \times 86.7}} = 1.602 \times 0.6398 = 1.02$$

Roughly double the Cv found for the 0.15 s requirement, consistent with the inverse relationship between fill time and required flow.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 4, Problem 2 (design decision): valve Cv is adequate but fill time still misses target</summary>

A newly commissioned station's directional valve is confirmed to have Cv well above the calculated requirement, yet the cylinder still isn't filling within the specified time on the shop floor. What are the likely causes, given everything else covered in this chapter?

**Answer:** If the valve itself has adequate Cv, the bottleneck has moved somewhere else in the air path. Likely causes, in roughly the order worth checking: (1) undersized or excessively long tubing between the valve and cylinder — Design Task 4's own guidance flagged this as the point where upsizing the valve stops helping; (2) a meter-out flow-control (speed-control) valve installed at the cylinder port set too restrictive, deliberately throttling the fill; (3) the regulator or FRL upstream of the valve sagging under the flow demand (Design Task 5), meaning the valve never actually sees the assumed supply pressure during the fill; (4) a leak or other parasitic draw elsewhere on the same branch reducing available pressure/flow at the moment this cylinder fires. This is a good example of why a fill-time miss isn't automatically a "valve too small" problem — the valve is only one link in the chain this chapter built.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 5, Problem 1 (plug-in): FRL sizing for a larger branch</summary>

A branch feeds five cylinders, each averaging 2.2 SCFM, with a 40% oversize margin specified. Find the required FRL rated flow.

**Solution:**

$$Q_{branch} = 5 \times 2.2 = 11.0\ \text{SCFM} \qquad Q_{FRL,required} = 11.0 \times 1.40 = 15.4\ \text{SCFM}$$

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 5, Problem 2 (design decision): a maintenance tech wants to add a lubricator</summary>

A maintenance technician, following habits from an older plant, wants to add an in-line lubricator to a branch feeding modern, pre-lubricated cylinders in a dry-goods (non-washdown) automotive plant, "just to be safe." Do you agree, and how would you explain your answer?

**Answer:** No — per this chapter's decision framework, a lubricator isn't a harmless "extra margin" the way an oversized cylinder bore might be; it actively works against pre-lubricated components by washing out their factory grease over time, and it locks the branch into needing lubricated air indefinitely (with the associated risk of accidentally cross-connecting a lube-free branch elsewhere in the plant). The correct response is to check the specific cylinder and valve manufacturer's datasheets: if none of them call for lubricated air, the answer is no lubricator, regardless of what practice was standard at a previous plant. This is a good moment to point out that "just to be safe" isn't automatically true margin — Design Task 1's oversize guideline is safe because more bore area only costs money and air, while an unnecessary lubricator can actively degrade the very components it's meant to help.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 6, Problem 1 (plug-in): leak cost at a smaller orifice</summary>

Using the same $0.28/1000 SCF rate, estimate the annual cost of a smaller 1.5 mm leak, given published leak-rate charts suggest roughly 6 SCFM continuous flow for that orifice size at 6 bar.

**Solution:**

$$\text{Annual SCF} = 6 \times 60 \times 24 \times 365 = 3\,153\,600\ \text{SCF/yr}$$

$$\text{Annual cost} = \frac{3\,153\,600}{1000} \times 0.28 \approx \$883/\text{yr}$$

Smaller than the chapter's 3 mm leak example (about $3,238/yr), but still a meaningful, entirely avoidable annual cost for a single leaking fitting.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 6, Problem 2 (design decision): where to spend a limited compressed-air budget</summary>

A plant's maintenance budget can fund either a leak-detection survey (typically finding 15-30 leaks of varying size in a plant this size) or a project to right-size six oversized cylinders identified during a design review. Which would you recommend prioritizing first, and why?

**Answer:** Prioritize the leak survey first, for the same reason this chapter's own comparison found the single leak example outweighing the entire fleet's cylinder-oversizing waste: leaks are typically the larger, faster-growing cost driver in a compressed air system, because they accumulate silently and continuously across the whole plant, while oversized components are a fixed, one-time inefficiency that was decided once. A leak survey also tends to have a faster payback (leaks are often cheap to fix — a fitting or valve replacement — once found) than redesigning and replacing six cylinders. That said, this isn't an either/or in the long run: right-sizing new designs going forward (this chapter's Design Tasks 1-4) prevents the next generation of oversized components from ever entering the system, so the real answer is "leak survey first, then build right-sizing discipline into the design process so there's less to retrofit later."

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 7, Problem 1 (plug-in): re-weighting for a simple clamp application</summary>

Using the same electric/pneumatic scores as the worked example, but with weights of 10% precision, 5% multi-position, 10% force consistency, 15% energy cost, 35% purchase cost, 25% robustness (a simple, harsh-environment, two-position clamp), which option wins?

**Solution:**

$$Score_{electric} = 0.10(5)+0.05(5)+0.10(5)+0.15(4)+0.35(2)+0.25(3) = 3.10$$

$$Score_{pneumatic} = 0.10(2)+0.05(1)+0.10(2)+0.15(2)+0.35(5)+0.25(5) = 3.80$$

Pneumatic wins under these cost/robustness-weighted priorities — consistent with this chapter's own clamp and pick-and-place examples.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design Task 7, Problem 2 (design decision): a borderline case</summary>

A packaging-line diverter needs to move between three fixed positions (not fully programmable, but more than two), running in a moderately dusty environment, with no unusual precision requirement. Electric or pneumatic, and what middle-ground option from this chapter's guidance is worth considering?

**Answer:** This sits close to the boundary this chapter flagged: three fixed positions is more than a standard two-position pneumatic cylinder handles directly, but the positions are fixed at design time (not runtime-programmable) and precision demands are modest — exactly the profile this chapter described for a mechanically-indexed multi-position pneumatic axis (a cylinder with a rotating or sliding multi-stop mechanism) as a lower-cost middle ground between simple pneumatics and a full electric axis. Given the dusty environment favors pneumatics' robustness and the requirement doesn't need the runtime flexibility or tight precision that would favor electric, a multi-stop pneumatic solution is worth quoting alongside a full electric axis before defaulting to either extreme — the deciding factor would likely come down to whether three positions is genuinely fixed for the life of the equipment (favoring pneumatic) or likely to need a fourth position or repositioning down the road (favoring electric's software-only reconfigurability).

</details>

## Open-Ended Design Scenario

<details>
<summary>Capstone: pneumatic clamp-and-transfer station for a dairy packaging line</summary>

A dairy processing plant is adding a clamp-and-transfer station to its cup-filling line. The station has two pneumatic axes:

**Clamp cylinder:** Extends horizontally to hold a tray of filled cups square against a locating fence while a robotic case-packer loads the tray, then retracts to release it. Required clamp force (extend stroke): 420 N. Required release force (retract stroke, overcoming friction and a light return spring): 90 N. Line pressure is 6 bar. The plant runs three shifts, 6 days/week, roughly 4,700 h/year.

**Lift-and-lower transfer cylinder:** A separate vertical cylinder, mounted rod-down, lowers an empty tray carrier onto the conveyor (extend, 150 N required) and lifts the loaded tray carrier clear (retract, 480 N required, governed by the annulus area). Stroke: 120 mm. The station cycles at 24 cycles/minute.

The plant's engineering standard requires stainless steel, IP69K washdown-rated pneumatic components throughout, consistent with CFIA sanitary design expectations for equipment operating near open product.

Using the methods developed in this chapter:

1. For each cylinder, work through Design Task 1: find the minimum required area on the governing stroke, apply the 25-50% oversize guideline, and select a standard ISO 15552 bore/rod combination for each (32/12, 40/16, 50/20, and 63/20 mm are all available options — you may need to check more than one candidate per cylinder, the way the chapter's own example did).
2. For the transfer cylinder, apply Design Task 2: using a combined efficiency factor of 0.75 (a washdown environment with somewhat longer stainless tubing runs than the chapter's automotive example), verify actual retract force still clears the 480 N requirement.
3. For the transfer cylinder, apply Design Task 3: calculate free-air consumption in SCFM at the specified 24 cycles/min cycle rate.
4. For the transfer cylinder's extend stroke, apply Design Task 4: if the process requires the lower stroke to complete within 0.20 s, calculate the required valve Cv (use the same pressure/temperature assumptions as the chapter's worked example: 6 bar supply, 15 psi valve drop, 530 °R).
5. Apply Design Task 5's decision framework: specify the FRL for this station (both cylinders on one branch), and make and justify the lubrication call given the washdown/food environment.
6. Apply Design Task 6: using the plant's actual 4,700 h/year operating schedule and the industry rule-of-thumb $/1000 SCF rate, estimate this station's annual compressed-air cost, and identify one design decision from steps 1-5 that would most directly reduce it.
7. Apply Design Task 7's framework only if asked to justify the choice of pneumatics at all for this station: build a short weighted decision matrix defending pneumatic over electric for a clamp-and-transfer application in a washdown dairy environment, using your own weights.

There's no single correct numeric answer — reasonable differences in assumed friction, oversize margin, and rounding to standard sizes will produce different (defensible) specifications. The goal is a documented sizing package, in the style of this chapter's worked examples, that could be handed to a pneumatic component distributor for an actual quotation.
